rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A man says his relatives sever ties, mistreat him, and answer his kindness with harm; the Prophet tells him to keep giving generously, promising divine support.
rows.anchor: ولكن جد بالفضل وصلهم؛ فإنه لن يزال معك ظهير من الله، عز وجل، ما كنت على ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir says this report is unique through this route but has corroboration through another route.
rows.anchor: تفرد به من هذا الوجه، وله شاهد

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن عمرو
rows.claim: The Prophet says kinship hangs from the Throne, and the true maintainer is the one who reconnects after relatives sever ties, not merely one who reciprocates.
rows.anchor: إن الرحم معلقة بالعرش، وليس الواصل بالمكافئ، ولكن الواصل الذي إذا قطعت رحمه وصلها

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن عمرو
rows.claim: A Prophetic report depicts kinship on Judgment Day with a spindle-like hook and fluent speech, joining those who maintained it and severing those who cut it.
rows.anchor: توضع الرحم يوم القيامة لها حجنة كحجنة المغزل، تتكلم بلسان طلق ذلق

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن عمرو
rows.claim: The Prophet urges mercy to earthly people and says God joins those who preserve kinship and cuts off those who sever it; al-Tirmidhi grades the report hasan sahih, and Ibn Kathir notes its first-link transmission.
rows.anchor: وهذا هو الذي يروى بتسلسل الأولية (12) ، وقال الترمذي: حسن صحيح

rows.speaker: عبد الرحمن بن عوف
rows.claim: A divine report says God is al-Rahman, created kinship from His name, and joins whoever maintains it while cutting off whoever severs it.
rows.anchor: أنا الرحمن، خلقت الرحم وشققت لها من اسمي، فمن يصلها أصله، ومن يقطعها أقطعه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir says the preceding report was unique by one route but also transmitted by Ahmad through al-Zuhri and by Abu Dawud and al-Tirmidhi through other routes; many reports support the point.
rows.anchor: ورواه أحمد أيضا من حديث الزهري، عن أبي سلمة، عن الرداد- أو أبي الرداد-عن عبد الرحمن بن عوف

rows.speaker: سلمان
rows.claim: A Prophetic report compares souls to assembled troops: those who recognize one another unite, while those who do not recognize one another differ.
rows.anchor: الأرواح جنود مجندة، فما تعارف منها ائتلف

rows.speaker: سلمان
rows.claim: A Prophetic warning says that when tongues agree while hearts hate and relatives sever ties, God curses people, making them deaf and blinding their sight.
rows.anchor: إذا ظهر القول، وخزن العمل، وائتلفت الألسنة، وتباغضت القلوب، وقطع كل ذي رحم رحمه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah was revealed as the Prophet returned from Hudaybiyyah in Dhul-Qadah, year six, after the Meccans blocked his pilgrimage and agreed he would return that year and come the next.
rows.anchor: نزلت هذه السورة الكريمة لما رجع رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم من الحديبية في ذي القعدة من سنة ست من الهجرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although some Companions, including Umar, disliked the truce, God called it a manifest victory because of its benefit and eventual outcome.
rows.anchor: وجعل ذلك الصلح فتحا باعتبار ما فيه من المصلحة، وما آل الأمر إليه

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masud says people count the conquest of Mecca as the victory, while his group counted the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah as the victory.
rows.anchor: إنكم تعدون الفتح فتح مكة، ونحن نعد الفتح صلح الحديبية

rows.speaker: جابر
rows.claim: Jabir says the Companions counted no event as the victory except the day of Hudaybiyyah.
rows.anchor: ما كنا نعد الفتح إلا يوم الحديبية

rows.speaker: البراء
rows.claim: Al-Bara says they counted the Hudaybiyyah pledge as the victory; he recalls the Prophet’s water blessing at the depleted well, while acknowledging Mecca’s conquest was also a victory.
rows.anchor: وقد كان فتح مكة فتحا، ونحن نعد الفتح بيعة الرضوان يوم الحديبية، كنا مع رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم أربع عشرة مائة

rows.speaker: عمر بن الخطاب
rows.claim: After Umar worried that the Prophet’s silence might signal revelation about him, a herald summoned him and the Prophet announced a surah dearer to him than the world and all it contains.
rows.anchor: سورة هي أحب إلي من الدنيا وما فيها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Bukhari, al-Tirmidhi, and al-Nasa'i transmit Umar’s report through Malik; Ali ibn al-Madini calls its Medinan chain good and says it is found only among them.
rows.anchor: وقال علي بن المديني: هذا إسناد مديني [جيد]

rows.speaker: أنس بن مالك
rows.claim: Anas says the forgiveness verse was revealed when the Prophet returned from Hudaybiyyah; the Prophet called it dearer than the earth, and the Companions congratulated him.
rows.anchor: نزلت على النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: أنس بن مالك
rows.claim: When the Companions asked what God would do for them, the verse promising believing men and women gardens through great triumph was revealed.
rows.anchor: فماذا يفعل بنا؟ فنزلت عليه: {ليدخل المؤمنين والمؤمنات جنات} حتى بلغ: {فوزا عظيما}

rows.speaker: مجمع بن جارية الأنصاري
rows.claim: After Hudaybiyyah, the Prophet recited the revelation at Kura al-Ghamim and swore to a Companion who asked that it was indeed a victory.
rows.anchor: والذي نفس محمد بيده، إنه لفتح

rows.speaker: مجمع بن جارية الأنصاري
rows.claim: Khaybar’s spoils were reserved for those who had attended Hudaybiyyah; nobody else joined them in that allocation.
rows.anchor: فقسمت خيبر على أهل الحديبية لم يدخل معهم فيها أحد إلا من شهد الحديبية

rows.speaker: مجمع بن جارية الأنصاري
rows.claim: The Prophet divided the Khaybar force into eighteen shares: the army numbered fifteen hundred mounted men, with two shares for a horseman and one for a foot soldier.
rows.anchor: فقسمها رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم على ثمانية عشر سهما، وكان الجيش ألفا وخمسمائة فارس

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن مسعود
rows.claim: Returning from Hudaybiyyah, the Companions slept past sunrise; the Prophet told them to do as usual, as anyone who sleeps or forgets should, then revelation came while they traveled.
rows.anchor: لما أقبلنا من الحديبية أعرسنا فنمنا

rows.speaker: المغيرة بن شعبة
rows.claim: When asked why he prayed until his feet swelled despite his forgiveness, the Prophet answered that he should be a grateful servant; al-Bukhari, Muslim, and the other compilers except Abu Dawud transmit it.
rows.anchor: فقيل له: أليس قد غفر الله لك ما تقدم من ذنبك وما تأخر

rows.speaker: عائشة
rows.claim: Aisha reports that the Prophet prayed until his feet cracked and gave the same answer that he should be a grateful servant; Muslim transmits her report.
rows.anchor: يا رسول الله، أتصنع هذا وقد غفر لك الله ما تقدم من ذنبك وما تأخر

rows.speaker: أنس
rows.claim: Anas reports that the Prophet stood until his feet or legs swelled and answered that he should be a grateful servant; Ibn Kathir calls this route unusual.
rows.anchor: قام رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم حتى تورمت قدماه -أو قال ساقاه-فقيل له: أليس قد غفر الله لك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The manifest victory is the Hudaybiyyah truce: it brought abundant good, safety, gathering, conversation between believers and unbelievers, and the spread of beneficial knowledge and faith.
rows.anchor: المراد به صلح الحديبية فإنه حصل بسببه خير جزيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Forgiveness of past and future sin is a special honor for the Prophet, not a reward promised to anyone else; Ibn Kathir calls him the most obedient, upright, and perfect of humanity.
rows.anchor: هذا من خصائصه -صلوات الله وسلامه عليه-

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet’s obedience to God included honoring sacred limits and accepting the truce; when his camel knelt, he said its restrainer was the one who restrained the elephant, then promised to grant any request honoring God’s sanctities.
rows.anchor: قال حين بركت به الناقة: "حبسها حابس الفيل"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God completes the Prophet’s favor in this world and the next, and guides him through the great law and upright religion He legislates.
rows.anchor: بما يشرعه لك من الشرع العظيم والدين القويم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Asakir gives an extended account of Subaygh; Ibn Abbas, Ibn Umar, Mujahid, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Hasan, Qatada, and al-Suddi share the interpretation, with no alternative reported by Ibn Jarir or Ibn Abi Hatim.
rows.anchor: ولم يحك ابن جرير وابن أبي حاتم غير ذلك

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some interpret the scatterers as winds and the burden-bearing ones as clouds, since clouds carry water.
rows.anchor: وبالحاملات وقرا: السحاب كما تقدم؛ لأنها تحمل الماء

rows.speaker: زيد بن عمرو بن نفيل
rows.claim: Zayd ibn Amr’s verse says clouds carry sweet, clear water, supporting the interpretation of the burden-bearers as clouds.
rows.anchor: له المزن تحمل عذبا زلالا

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: The majority identify the gently moving runners as ships sailing smoothly through water.
rows.anchor: فالمشهور عن الجمهور -كما تقدم-: أنها السفن، تجري ميسرة في الماء جريا سهلا

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some identify the runners as stars moving gently in their orbits, making the sequence rise from lower to higher created things.
rows.anchor: في أفلاكها، ليكون ذلك ترقيا من الأدنى إلى الأعلى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apportioners of affairs are angels above the stars, descending with God’s religious and cosmic commands.
rows.anchor: والمقسمات أمرا الملائكة فوق ذلك، تنزل بأوامر الله الشرعية والكونية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The oath affirms resurrection: what people are promised is truthful, and the reckoning will certainly occur.
rows.anchor: وهذا قسم من الله عز جل على وقوع المعاد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here al-din means reckoning, which is bound to take place.
rows.anchor: الحساب {لواقع} أي: لكائن لا محالة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas and the named early authorities interpret the heaven’s hubuk as its splendor, beauty, goodness, and evenness.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: ذات البهاء والجمال والحسن والاستواء

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Dahhak, al-Mihal ibn Amr, and others compare hubuk to the interwoven ripples or ridges in wind-struck water, sand, and crops.
rows.anchor: وقال الضحاك، والمنهال بن عمرو، وغيرهما: مثل تجعد الماء والرمل والزرع إذا ضربته الريح

rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A report from an unnamed Companion says a deceiving liar will come whose head has hubuk, which Ibn Jarir explains as curly texture.
rows.anchor: إن من ورائكم الكذاب المضل، وإن رأسه من ورائه حبك حبك

rows.speaker: أبو صالح
rows.claim: Abu Salih interprets hubuk as firmness.
rows.anchor: وعن أبي صالح: {ذات الحبك}

rows.speaker: خصيف
rows.claim: Khasif interprets hubuk as tightly woven or closely set.
rows.anchor: وقال خصيف: {ذات الحبك} : ذات الصفافة

rows.speaker: الحسن بن أبي الحسن البصري
rows.claim: Al-Hasan al-Basri says the heaven is patterned with stars.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن بن أبي الحسن البصري: {ذات الحبك}

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir rebukes the polytheists for worshipping idols and rivals and building shrines to imitate the Kaaba built by Abraham.
rows.anchor: يقول تعالى مقرعا للمشركين في عبادتهم الأصنام والأنداد والأوثان، واتخاذهم لها البيوت مضاهاة للكعبة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Lat was a white inscribed rock with a curtained shrine, attendants, and a revered enclosure at Taif; Thaqif and its followers boasted of it after Quraysh.
rows.anchor: صخرة بيضاء منقوشة، وعليها بيت بالطائف له أستار وسدنة، وحوله فناء معظم عند أهل الطائف

rows.speaker: ابن جرير
rows.claim: Ibn Jarir says the polytheists derived al-Lat’s name from Allah and treated it as a feminine form, an attribution Ibn Kathir condemns as exalted above God.
rows.anchor: فقالوا: اللات، يعنون مؤنثة منه

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, and al-Rabi ibn Anas read al-Lat with a doubled t and explain it as a man who prepared sawiq for pilgrims, whose grave was later worshipped.
rows.anchor: وحكي عن ابن عباس، ومجاهد، والربيع بن أنس: أنهم قرؤوا

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: A report in al-Bukhari likewise identifies al-Lat as a man who ground sawiq for pilgrims.
rows.anchor: قال: كان اللات رجلا يلت السويق، سويق الحاج

rows.speaker: ابن جرير
rows.claim: Ibn Jarir derives al-Uzza’s name from al-Aziz; its shrine was a revered tree with a building and curtains at Nakhlah between Mecca and Taif.
rows.anchor: وكذا العزى من العزيز. وكانت شجرة عليها بناء وأستار بنخلة، وهي بين مكة والطائف

rows.speaker: أبو سفيان
rows.claim: At Uhud, Abu Sufyan proclaimed Uzza’s allegiance; the Prophet instructed the Muslims to answer that God is their protector and the polytheists have no protector.
rows.anchor: كما قال أبو سفيان يوم أحد: لنا العزى ولا عزى لكم فقال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة
rows.claim: The Prophet says one who swears by al-Lat or al-Uzza should affirm God’s oneness, and one who invites a companion to gamble should give charity.
rows.anchor: من حلف فقال في حلفه: واللات والعزى، فليقل: لا إله إلا الله. ومن قال لصاحبه: تعال أقامرك، فليتصدق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir treats the oath as a slip of a tongue habituated in pre-Islamic times; when Sa'd swore by these idols, the Prophet taught him to renew tawhid, spit left three times, seek refuge from Satan, and not repeat it.
rows.anchor: لا إله إلا الله وحده لا شريك له، له الملك وله الحمد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Manat stood at al-Mushallal near Qudayd between Mecca and Medina; Khuzā'a, Aws, and Khazraj revered it and began their pilgrimage talbiya there.
rows.anchor: عند قديد، بين مكة والمدينة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arabia had other revered idols, but Ibn Kathir says these three alone were named because they were the most famous.
rows.anchor: وإنما أفرد هذه بالذكر لأنها أشهر من غيرها

rows.speaker: ابن إسحاق
rows.claim: Ibn Ishaq describes Arab shrines as Kaaba-like houses with attendants, offerings, circumambulation, and sacrifice, while their worshippers recognized the Kaaba’s superiority as Abraham’s sanctuary.
rows.anchor: وتطوف بها كطوفاتها بها، وتنحر عندها، وهي تعرف فضل الكعبة عليها

rows.speaker: ابن إسحاق
rows.claim: Uzza belonged to Quraysh and Banu Kinanah at Nakhlah, with its keepers from Banu Shayban of Sulaym, allies of Banu Hashim.
rows.anchor: فكانت لقريش وبني كنانة العزى بنخلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet sent Khalid ibn al-Walid to destroy Uzza, and Khalid chanted that God had humiliated it.
rows.anchor: يا عز، كفرانك لا سبحانك … إني رأيت الله قد أهانك

rows.speaker: أبو الطفيل
rows.claim: Abu al-Tufayl reports that Khalid first cut Uzza’s three trees and demolished its structure; the Prophet sent him back, where he killed the naked woman embodying the idol, then identified her as Uzza.
rows.anchor: ارجع فإنك لم تصنع شيئا

rows.speaker: ابن إسحاق
rows.claim: Ibn Ishaq says al-Lat belonged to Thaqif at Taif and was tended by Banu Mu'tab; the Prophet sent al-Mughira ibn Shu'ba and Abu Sufyan to demolish it and build a mosque in its place.
rows.anchor: وكانت اللات لثقيف بالطائف، وكان سدنتها وحجابها بنى معتب

rows.speaker: ابن إسحاق
rows.claim: Manat belonged to the Aws, Khazraj, and their co-religionists in Yathrib by the shore near al-Mushallal at Qudayd; the Prophet sent Abu Sufyan to destroy it, though another account names Ali.
rows.anchor: قال ابن إسحاق: وكانت مناة للأوس والخزرج ومن دان بدينهم من أهل يثرب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dhu al-Khalasa belonged to Daws, Khath'am, Bajila, and neighboring Arabs at Tabala; it was called the Yemeni Kaaba, while Mecca’s Kaaba was the Syrian Kaaba, and Jarir demolished it.
rows.anchor: لدوس وخثعم وبجيلة، ومن كان ببلادهم من العرب بتبالة

rows.speaker: ابن هشام
rows.claim: Fals belonged to Tayy and nearby tribes; Ibn Hisham says the Prophet sent Ali to destroy it and awarded him its two swords, al-Rasub and al-Mikhdham.
rows.anchor: نفله أياهما رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: ابن إسحاق
rows.claim: Ibn Ishaq says Himyar and Yemenis had a shrine called Riyam in Sana'a, where two rabbis accompanying Tubba found and killed a black dog and demolished the shrine.
rows.anchor: وكان لحمير وأهل اليمن بيت بصنعاء يقال له: ريام

rows.speaker: ابن إسحاق
rows.claim: Rida was a shrine of Banu Rabi'a ibn Ka'b; al-Mustawghir composed a poem about its destruction, and Ibn Hisham says the poet lived 330 years and preserves further verses about his lifespan.
rows.anchor: ولها يقول المستوغر بن ربيعة بن كعب بن سعد حين هدمها في الإسلام

rows.speaker: الأعشى
rows.claim: Dhu al-Kaabat at Sindad belonged to Bakr and Taghlib ibn Wa'il and Iyad; al-A'sha names it in a poem.
rows.anchor: والبيت ذو الكعبات من سنداد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The rebuke asks whether the polytheists assign God a daughter while reserving sons for themselves; even among creatures that would be an unjust, foolish division, so attributing it to God is worse.
rows.anchor: أتجعلون له ولدا، وتجعلون ولده أنثى، وتختارون لأنفسكم الذكور، فلو اقتسمتم أنتم ومخلوق مثلكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The idols are names invented by people and their ancestors without divine proof; their only support is conjecture, inherited approval, self-interest in leadership, and veneration of forefathers, despite clear guidance from God’s messengers.
rows.anchor: {ما أنزل الله بها من سلطان}

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their reliance on ancestral opinion and personal advantage supplies no evidence, and they refused the clear truth and decisive proof brought by the messengers.
rows.anchor: ليس لهم مستند إلا حسن ظنهم بآبائهم الذين سلكوا هذا المسلك الباطل قبلهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A person does not obtain everything he wishes; the verse is linked to the statement that neither your wishes nor those of the People of the Book determine the outcome, and claims of guidance or desire do not guarantee it.
rows.anchor: ليس كل من تمنى خيرا حصل له

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة
rows.claim: The Prophet tells anyone who wishes to consider carefully what he wishes, since he does not know what will be recorded for him; Ahmad alone transmits this report.
rows.anchor: إذا تمنى أحدكم فلينظر ما يتمنى، فإنه لا يدري ما يكتب له من أمنيته
